quests.goal: Wake face-down on the Barrow Flat at the first ebb, with a lead passage-token closed in your fist, and stand up.
Cross the cairn field to the shelf where the flat meets the cliff, staying inside the three iron tide-stakes. Inside the line is walking; outside it the mud takes you.
Speak to Emeric Tallow on the last dry shelf, who has lit a shore-lamp for the dead every night for fifty-one years, and hear what the three tolls mean.
Climb the cut ledge on the seaward face, reading the wall rather than the floor, and cross the fallen section where the iron brackets bend down into nothing.

Take the rope from the store cut into the cliff, where the priory kept the handrail it stopped replacing. It is salt-hard, it is the rope the bell will need, and the road passes straight through the store.
Enter Halgrave through the sea-broken hole in the gatehouse wall and come down inside the gate passage, behind a portcullis that is shut against the shore you woke on.
Work the winch on the passage's inner side and raise the portcullis, opening the rock's front door from behind it — and watch the sea come up over the flat you crossed an hour ago.
Cross the raised stone spine over the drowned outer ward to the water-gate tower, past the two weed pinches, with the waders standing in the water on both sides.
The tower's ground door is barred from inside. Climb the ruined arcade top and enter the tower at shutter height instead.
Descend inside the water-gate tower and lift the bar off its ground door from within — the door that told you, from the far side, that it did not open from there.

Cross the roofless chapel ward and put down the Two Sextons, who carried the dead in from the boats and still work as a pair, while Sister Ide walks her round through the middle of it and does not stop.
Unbar the one intact door on the rock from the chapel side. Through it as it swings, the drowned ward below is going under the flood — on the route you have just made unnecessary.
Enter the one building on Halgrave with its roof still on, and beat Housecarl Ridd on the open hall floor — the man who broke the belfry stair on an order and is not sorry.

Speak to Prior Ancel Wray, who ordered the two tolls and has not left his chair since. He gives up the two facts you need without fear, because they have never been dangerous before: the tongue went down the cistern well, and the belfry stair is broken at the first flight.
Take the keep stair down under everything you have already crossed and reach the well head in the cistern. The climb's last move is a descent, and the sea is going out ahead of you as you come down.

Put down the Founder beside the well he threw the tongue into — the man who cast Mercy, was made to strike its tongue out, and came down after it. He falls in ankle-deep water, and the water goes out from under him.

Take the bell's tongue out of the drained well: copper, the length of a man, lying in silt that has not seen air since the year it was thrown there. It is not awarded and not unlocked. The sea uncovered it, for about two hours, once in fifty-one years.
Break the iron grate outward from the cistern side — the only route back up — and come out onto the drowned ward with no water in it, on a floor nobody has stood on for fifty-one years.
Climb the cobbled ramp between the collapsed low buildings of the upper ward to the foot of the tower, where the whole climb is finally visible as one shape.

The household broke the first flight of the belfry stair so that nobody would go up. Lay the two missing tread courses at the head of the flight with the rope carried from the cliff road. Both courses or neither: one alone leaves the tower shut.

Odo Ferrier is on the stairhead below the belfry floor and means to be the last hand himself. Beaten, he sits down on the stair and lets you past; he cannot be killed and he does not want to kill you.

Fit the tongue and bend the rope on in the open belfry, with whoever you have brought this far standing around the bell. Mercy answers the last hand, and the last hand is yours: three, two, or the frame.
